label: Donini: Aristotle's counter-argument against determinism follows a parallel structure to

metadata.topic: Aristotle's response to determinism in de Interpretatione 9
metadata.stance: Aristotle's counter-argument against determinism follows a parallel structure to the deterministic argument: denying the futility of deliberation (c), then denying that everything happens by necessity (b), and finally denying wholesale application of bivalence/excluded middle to future singulars (a). The deterministic argument's fundamental flaw is that it violates the correspondence principle by moving from logoi to pragmata rather than vice versa.

label: Donini: The future's status as pragma is problematic for Aristotle's correspondence prin

metadata.topic: Status of future contingents as pragmata
metadata.stance: The future's status as pragma is problematic for Aristotle's correspondence principle; if the future is not a pragma in the same way as present/past, this affects whether truth can be spoken of concerning the future. Aristotle does not absolutely prohibit speaking of truth for the future, but restricts rather than abolishes the logical principle (ouk homoiōs, not oudamēs).

label: Dihle: Greek philosophical theology from Plato and Aristotle onward did not conceive of

metadata.topic: Greek philosophical theology and divine will
metadata.stance: Greek philosophical theology from Plato and Aristotle onward did not conceive of divine will as arbitrary or unpredictable intention; rather, divine activity manifests perfect rationality, order, and beauty. The demiurge realizes only what reason shows to be possible and always chooses the best. No separate will spontaneously interferes with the rational programming of reality.

label: Dihle: Jewish and early Christian theology conceived of creation as dependent solely on

metadata.topic: Jewish and Christian conception of divine will vs. Greek philosophy
metadata.stance: Jewish and early Christian theology conceived of creation as dependent solely on the arbitrary will of the divine creator, who could transform a lump of earth into any creature. This conception was preferable to Epicurean chance but incompatible with Greek rational cosmology. This fundamental difference between Greek and biblical thought becomes central to the historical development of the 'will' concept.
supporting_evidence: Galen De partibus corporis humani (on eyelashes and creation)

label: Dihle: Greek philosophical tradition, both Stoic and Platonic, rejected the popular rel

metadata.topic: Prayer and divine immutability in Greek philosophy
metadata.stance: Greek philosophical tradition, both Stoic and Platonic, rejected the popular religious notion that prayer could influence or change God's intention. Such change would imply imperfection, since God could not improve on his own rationality. Prayer served only to ascertain identity between cosmic and human reason (Stoics) or to contribute to fuller cognition of God (Platonists).
supporting_evidence: Cleanthes ap. Seneca Epistulae 41.1, Quaestiones naturales 2.35

label: Löhr: Irenaeus employed well-known philosophical anti-determinist arguments against th

metadata.topic: Irenaeus's anti-determinist arguments and their philosophical sources
metadata.stance: Irenaeus employed well-known philosophical anti-determinist arguments against the Valentinians, particularly the 'lazy argument' (ἀργὸς λόγος) originally used by the Sceptical Academy against Stoic determinism, and the argument that determinism removes moral responsibility (praise/blame). These were widespread in second-century philosophy (Alkinoos, Alexander of Aphrodisias) and theology (Justin Martyr).
supporting_evidence: Irenaeus, Adversus haereses II.29.1-3 (superfluity of faith and Saviour's descent if souls saved by substance)
Irenaeus, Adversus haereses IV.37.2 (natural goodness/badness and moral responsibility)
Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics (source for praise/blame argument)

label: Löhr: Clement, despite having first-hand knowledge of Valentinian sources and understa

metadata.topic: Clement of Alexandria's adaptation of heresiological determinism
metadata.stance: Clement, despite having first-hand knowledge of Valentinian sources and understanding that 'saved by nature' referred to the pneumatic element, nevertheless adopted and intensified Irenaeus's heresiological picture. He discovered 'gnostic determinism' even in innocent-seeming fragments of Basilides and Isidorus, and described Gnostic determinism in Stoic terminology without making the Stoic-heresy connection explicit.

engages_with_scholars.note: Clement uses Irenaeus's heresiological picture and arguments but develops them in his own way

supporting_evidence: Clement of Alexandria, Stromata II.10.1ff (explicit argument against gnostic determinism)
Clement of Alexandria, Stromata II.111.3-4 (faculty of assent and spiritual struggle)
Basilides fragment: faith as 'assent' (συγκατάθεσις) to things not perceived

label: Löhr: Clement paradoxically employed Stoic philosophical concepts—particularly the fac

metadata.topic: Clement's use of Stoic concepts against determinism
metadata.stance: Clement paradoxically employed Stoic philosophical concepts—particularly the faculty of assent (συγκατάθεσις/ἡγεμονικόν)—to combat what he perceived as Gnostic determinism, drawing on Chrysippus's distinction between internal and external causes. However, this was a weak argument because Basilides himself had used 'assent' for faith, and because a nature-based determinism could simply identify nature with the perfected faculty of rational assent.
supporting_evidence: Chrysippus (on internal/external causes and primary/secondary antecedent causes)
Basilides fragment on faith as συγκατάθεσις

label: Löhr: Origen took up Clement's work at its weakest point and expanded the charge of Gn

metadata.topic: Origen's expansion of the determinism charge to Marcion
metadata.stance: Origen took up Clement's work at its weakest point and expanded the charge of Gnostic determinism to include Marcion alongside Valentinus and Basilides, forming a standard trio of determinist heretics. Origen developed Clement's emphasis on the soul's faculty of moral choice/assent, defending human freedom against both the extreme that denies all external influence and the extreme that blames inborn character.

engages_with_scholars.note: Origen takes up the problem where Clement left it, particularly the weakness of using assent against nature-based determinism

supporting_evidence: Origen's repeated references to Valentinus, Basilides, and Marcion as determinist trio

label: Cary: Plato developed the concept of a rational part of the soul that governs lower, p

metadata.topic: Plato on rational governance of the soul and freedom
metadata.stance: Plato developed the concept of a rational part of the soul that governs lower, passionate parts; this capacity for rational judgment over passion is foundational to Western philosophy's concept of human freedom. Animals lack this rational control, while humans can choose to act on rational judgment rather than passion.
supporting_evidence: Plato, Republic, 439c (thirsty man who realizes he ought not to drink)
Plato, Republic, 430d-445e (analogy of divided soul developed at length)

metadata.stance: The mythic conception of fate (from Latin fatum, 'what is said') is the crucial precursor to modern determinism. metadata.topic: Distinction between metaphysical and legal-practical issues about free will
metadata.stance: Courts do not need to settle the metaphysical problem of free will and determinism, but do need workable ideas of when human freedom and responsibility are compromised by coercion or ignorance. The question 'Was it really impossible for Oedipus to have escaped his fate?' is not court-decidable, but courts must distinguish crimes of passion from deliberate acts.

metadata.topic: Historical threats to free will
metadata.stance: What is meant by freedom has depended on what threatens to undermine it: originally fate, later force of circumstances, coercion, causal nexus of physical world, providence, grace of God, and nature of motivation itself. In modern philosophy the best name is determinism, which has precursors in medieval predestination and ancient fate.

metadata.topic: Tensions in Aristotle's own position on necessity and causality

label: Kowalski: Similarities: both believe free will can exist in a divinely determined world, a

metadata.topic: comparison of Paul and Epictetus on free will
metadata.stance: Similarities: both believe free will can exist in a divinely determined world, and human volition requires continuous education and subordination to God's will. Differences: Epictetus has a natural image of deity to be imitated in human pursuit of freedom, while Paul has a genuinely relational, corporeal and emotive character of free will; Paul's psycho-somatic nature of human personality and will invites dialogue with modern science but must be carried out cautiously due to different methodologies, transcendent deity, and Christological foundation.

metadata.topic: Comparison between Middle Platonist and Stoic fate theories
metadata.stance: The Middle Platonist theory of fate is considerably closer to the Stoic account than generally acknowledged. Both accept that events in the cosmos follow one another with predictable regularity according to antecedent causes. The crucial difference is that Platonists (unlike Stoics) insist that the cosmos itself need not have been this way—no sublunary event is fated absolutely.

Human choices, like all sublunary events, are fated as consequences of prior causes, but not absolutely—this preserves responsibility without requiring spontaneous uncaused action.

metadata.topic: Epicurus as 'first libertarian' / inventor of free will problem
metadata.stance: Epicurus has been mistakenly hailed as the first person to discover the free will problem and offer a libertarian solution. While Epicurus believes freedom and determinism are incompatible and denies determinism to preserve freedom, he was not formulating the traditional problem of free will and determinism. Epicurus was pivotal in the historical development of libertarian free will, but only because later philosophers appropriated and reshaped his position; he himself would have repudiated the libertarian conception of freedom of the will that later developed.

metadata.topic: Swerve and collisions / swerve and fate
metadata.stance: The swerve's role in preserving freedom from fate is not through providing indeterministic gaps for volition, but rather through ensuring that atomic collisions have non-necessitated origins, thereby undermining Democritean fatalism at the cosmological level. The swerve saves us from fate not by making individual actions undetermined but by ensuring that the causal history of the cosmos is not fully necessitated from eternity.

label: Acosta López de Mesa: Rejects the mainstream scholarly view (following Dihle and Frede) that there is

metadata.topic: origin of free will in ancient philosophy
metadata.stance: Rejects the mainstream scholarly view (following Dihle and Frede) that there is no notion of free will in ancient Greek philosophy; argues that Aristotle has a notion of free will that is broader and more effective than the Stoic intellectualist one

engages_with_scholars.note: Direct critique of Frede's claim that free will originates from the Stoic tradition, particularly from Epictetus; criticizes his 'intellectualist' conception and his method of looking for free will as if searching for a 'piece of gold' or a specific word
Critiques Dihle's claim in 'The Theory of Will in Classical Antiquity' that the concept of will originated in Saint Augustine as a third entity capable of choosing between good and evil

supporting_evidence: Aristotle's theory of the soul with rational and irrational parts
Aristotle's account of akrasia (acting wrong knowing what is good)
Epictetus's notion of will as 'ability of the mind or of reason to make choices and decisions'

label: Acosta López de Mesa: Aristotle's notion of free will is superior to the Stoic intellectualist concept

metadata.topic: Aristotle's notion of free will vs. Stoic intellectualism
metadata.stance: Aristotle's notion of free will is superior to the Stoic intellectualist conception because it genuinely explains the possibility of choosing evil; the Stoic moral intellectualism fails on this point since for them we always choose the good, and evil is merely accidental ignorance

engages_with_scholars.note: Frede claims Aristotle has a notion of choice but no notion of will or freedom; Acosta López de Mesa argues this is mistaken and that Frede is 'blind' to the limitations of Stoic intellectualism
Shares Plato's and Aristotle's rejection of Socratic intellectualism; their partition of the soul was raised against Socrates' view that humans act wrong only by ignorance

supporting_evidence: Aristotle's theory of soul with three parts: one rational and two irrational
Aristotle's account of akrasia: human beings can act wrong knowing what is good and convenient for them
Plato's and Aristotle's response to Socratic intellectualism

label: Acosta López de Mesa: The Stoic intellectualist free will, originating from Epictetus's combination of

metadata.topic: Stoic conception of free will and its limitations
metadata.stance: The Stoic intellectualist free will, originating from Epictetus's combination of will and freedom (exousia autopragias), is limited because it cannot genuinely explain choosing evil; for Stoics, all human impressions are rational and there are no irrational desires in adults, making evil merely a product of ignorance

engages_with_scholars.note: Accepts Frede's interpretation of Stoicism as 'very plausible' but argues it is insufficient and that Frede fails to recognize its limitations; the Stoics returned to Socratic intellectualism that Plato and Aristotle had rightly rejected

supporting_evidence: Epictetus's notion of will as 'ability of the mind or of reason to make choices and decisions'
Chrysippus's definition of freedom as 'having the ability to act one's own, to act at one's own discretion, to act on one's own account, to act independently'
Stoic claim that only the wise person is free and everybody else is a slave

metadata.topic: Alexander's shift to efficient cause: reasons and implications

label: Double: The traditional trichotomy of Hard Determinism/Soft Determinism/Libertarianism a

metadata.topic: methodological reframing of free will debate
metadata.stance: The traditional trichotomy of Hard Determinism/Soft Determinism/Libertarianism and the dichotomy of Incompatibilism vs. Compatibilism should be replaced by a framework with more possibilities that does not presuppose the free will problem is real. Distinguishing positive and negative claims of traditional Incompatibilists and Compatibilists yields four positions, and a fifth theory entails that 'free will' as objectively referential is logically incoherent.

engages_with_scholars.note: Van Inwagen's 1983 approach to defining free will is rejected as question-begging

label: Double: The label 'free will' or 'free choice' should be preferred over 'free action' be

metadata.topic: terminology: 'free will' vs. 'free action'
metadata.stance: The label 'free will' or 'free choice' should be preferred over 'free action' because the central concern is moral responsibility, which depends on whether choices are free. 'Free action' is perilous because it allows a Compatibilist gambit defining it as 'unimpeded action' (following Hobbes), committing the definist fallacy, and connotes tangential varieties of freedom (speech, religion).

engages_with_scholars.note: Chisholm cites Aquinas on the point that what matters for moral responsibility is whether choices are free
Hobbes's definition of 'free action' as 'unimpeded action' exemplifies the definist fallacy

label: Double: The preferred approach defines 'free choice' in a placeholder fashion neutral be

metadata.topic: placeholder definition of 'free choice'
metadata.stance: The preferred approach defines 'free choice' in a placeholder fashion neutral between competing theories, such as 'choices that, unless some excusing condition obtains, are sufficient to qualify their agents as morally responsible for the actions those choices (immediately) produce.' This avoids the definist fallacy of both Libertarian-biased and dual-definition approaches.

engages_with_scholars.note: Van Inwagen's 1983 Libertarian definition is rejected as encouraging the definist fallacy
Kane's 1985 Libertarian account illustrates the lack of consensus among Libertarians on where indeterminacy should occur

label: Double: The traditional trichotomy of Hard Determinism/Soft Determinism/Libertarianism a

metadata.topic: taxonomy of free will positions
metadata.stance: The traditional trichotomy of Hard Determinism/Soft Determinism/Libertarianism and the dichotomy of Incompatibilism vs. Compatibilism should be replaced by a framework with more possibilities that does not presuppose the free will problem is real. Distinguishing positive and negative claims of traditional incompatibilists and compatibilists yields four positions rather than two; looking at these claims differently produces a fifth theory that entails 'free will' is logically incoherent when taken to have objective reference.
metadata.source_file: [local-path] SHAL/04_Littérature_secondaire/07_Libre_arbitre_theologie/R. Double-How to Frame the Free Will Problem _OCR.md

label: Double: Double endorses a third approach: defining 'free choice' in a placeholder fashio

metadata.topic: definition of 'free will'/'free choice'
metadata.stance: Double endorses a third approach: defining 'free choice' in a placeholder fashion neutral between competing theories, specifically as 'choices that, unless some excusing condition obtains, are sufficient to qualify their agents as morally responsible for the actions those choices (immediately) produce.' He rejects defining 'free will' as indeterminate libertarian choices (approach 1) and as ambiguous between libertarian-style and compatibilist-style definitions (approach 2).

engages_with_scholars.note: Van Inwagen 1983's definition of free choices as indeterminate libertarian choices encourages the definist fallacy
Kane 1985's libertarian account is one of multiple incompatible libertarian definitions

metadata.source_file: [local-path] SHAL/04_Littérature_secondaire/07_Libre_arbitre_theologie/R. Double-How to Frame the Free Will Problem _OCR.md

label: Xie: Neither 'compatibilist' nor 'incompatibilist' adequately describes Kant, but inc

label: Xie: Kant's solution is not a success because making the effects of freedom part of t

metadata.topic: Success of Kant's solution to the free will problem
metadata.stance: Kant's solution is not a success because making the effects of freedom part of the field of appearance renders his solution incoherent and ambiguous; however, his attempt is groundbreaking because he at least separated freedom from the dominance of determinism

engages_with_scholars.note: Acknowledges Wood's more favorable assessment but disagrees with the conclusion that Kant successfully reconciled freedom and determinism

supporting_evidence: Kant, Critique of Pure Reason (on noumena and phenomena)

metadata.topic: Wood's interpretation of Kant as compatibilist
metadata.stance: Wood's interpretation contains contradictions: Wood acknowledges Kant believes freedom is incompatible with natural causation (which makes Kant an incompatibilist), yet still labels Kant a compatibilist because he thinks Kant succeeded in reconciling them; this reconciliation is questionable

engages_with_scholars.note: Direct engagement with Wood's 1984 paper 'Kant's Compatibilism'; quotes Wood's view that Kant's views 'do not fit neatly into the customary pigeonholes'

supporting_evidence: Wood, Allen: 'Kant's Compatibilism'. Self and Nature in Kant's Philosophy. Edited by Allen Wood. Ithaka, New York 1984, 73-101

metadata.topic: Kant's metaphysical division of two causalities
metadata.stance: Kant's solution depends on grounding phenomenal causality in noumenal causality, but this grounding is problematic: if actions are causally determined by natural causes as effects of empirical character, it is unclear how they can simultaneously be free as effects of intelligible character

engages_with_scholars.note: Uses Wood's formulation of the problem but argues it leads to incoherence rather than successful reconciliation

label: Guillon: The contemporary debate on free will is best understood through the traditional

metadata.topic: compatibilism vs incompatibilism
metadata.stance: The contemporary debate on free will is best understood through the traditional opposition between compatibilist and incompatibilist conceptions; compatibilism holds that free will is compatible with causal determinism, while incompatibilism (which has made a strong comeback since the 1970s-1980s) defends the intuition that determinism would deprive us of free will

engages_with_scholars.note: as source of compatibilist tradition
as source of compatibilist tradition
as last major French representative of contemporary approach to free will

label: Guillon: The free will debate is nearly as old as philosophy itself, with significant his

metadata.topic: historical scope of free will debate
metadata.stance: The free will debate is nearly as old as philosophy itself, with significant historical contests including Aristotle against the Megarians, Epicureans against Stoics, Augustine against Pelagius, Molina against Thomists, and Spinoza against Descartes; the core stakes have always been moral responsibility and anxiety about being deprived of it by some form of determinism

label: Guillon: In Anglo-American philosophy, the free will debate seemed definitively closed by

metadata.topic: Anglo-American revival of incompatibilism
metadata.stance: In Anglo-American philosophy, the free will debate seemed definitively closed by a broad compatibilist consensus since Hobbes and Hume, but the 1970s-1980s saw the reappearance of an extremely lively controversy where nearly the full variety of positions from other eras of philosophy's history could be found again

engages_with_scholars.note: as figure who helped close debate with compatibilist consensus
as figure who helped close debate with compatibilist consensus

label: Guillon: The contemporary approach to free will should not be dissuaded by the bimillenni

metadata.topic: methodological approach to contemporary free will
metadata.stance: The contemporary approach to free will should not be dissuaded by the bimillennial heritage from taking up the controversy anew with fresh arguments and in light of contemporary knowledge; historical approaches are valuable but should not prevent direct engagement with the problem

label: Guillon: The contemporary discussion on free will does not offer the homogeneity or conse

as contributor to volume

label: Hick: Hick adopts an Irenaean rather than Augustinian view of the Fall: humans were cr

label: Crouzel: Origen was not a philosopher but a theologian who subordinated philosophy to Chr

metadata.topic: Origen's relationship to Greek philosophy
metadata.stance: Origen was not a philosopher but a theologian who subordinated philosophy to Christian revelation; he regarded philosophy as 'surpassed' (périmée), like stars fading before the sun, destined to serve the 'divine philosophie' of Christianity

engages_with_scholars.note: Refutes de Faye's thesis that Origen paradoxically juxtaposed Greek philosopher and fervent Christian
Refutes Koch's similar thesis about Origen's paradoxical relationship to philosophy

supporting_evidence: Origen, Peri Archon (youthful work, to be treated cautiously)

label: Crouzel: Origen gives great importance to libre arbitre, partly because of its central ro

metadata.topic: Free will (libre arbitre) in Origen
metadata.stance: Origen gives great importance to libre arbitre, partly because of its central role in his anti-gnostic polemic; the gnostics' denial of free will and their predestination doctrines are key targets of Origen's theology
supporting_evidence: Quotation: 'doues de libre arbitre : les betes feroces elles-memes ont ete creees pour exercer l'homme' [Crouzel_1962.md:580]
Quotation: 'les biens dependant de notre libre arbitre avec ceux qui n'en dependent pas' [Crouzel_1962.md:1149]

label: Crouzel: Platonism dominates Origen's conception of libre arbitre; Platonism is Origen's

metadata.topic: Platonism and free will
metadata.stance: Platonism dominates Origen's conception of libre arbitre; Platonism is Origen's preferred philosophy for its doctrines leading the soul from the sensible to the invisible world, its teachings about beatitude near God, and its contempt for the transient, yet it remains insufficient compared to Christian revelation
supporting_evidence: Plato, various dialogues (doctrines of soul's ascent, beatitude, contempt for transient)

label: Crouzel: Origen achieves an original synthesis of two opposing patristic attitudes: the n

metadata.topic: Synthesis of patristic attitudes toward philosophy
metadata.stance: Origen achieves an original synthesis of two opposing patristic attitudes: the negative attitude (complete rupture with philosophy, represented by Tatien, Hermias, Irenaeus, Tertullian) and the sympathetic attitude (recognizing partial truths, represented by Justin, Clement); Origen's suspicion is greater than Clement's, but his engagement is deeper

engages_with_scholars.note: Justin as key predecessor: converted philosopher who kept sympathy for philosophy while acknowledging Christ alone as master; founded first Christian philosophy school with Logos doctrine and 'larcins' theory that Origen inherits
Origen's suspicion is greater than Clement's, but his engagement is deeper; Clement represents the sympathetic attitude toward philosophy

supporting_evidence: Justin Martyr, works (as predecessor with Logos doctrine and 'larcins' theory)
Quotation: 'Origene fait la synthese de ces deux attitudes et c'est la son originalite.' [Crouzel_1962.md:~7655]

label: Crouzel: According to Paul, pagans had authentic knowledge of God (Romans 1:18ff.) and re

metadata.topic: Pauline background for Christian use of philosophy
metadata.stance: According to Paul, pagans had authentic knowledge of God (Romans 1:18ff.) and received moral law in their nature (Romans 2:14ff.); Paul marked distance between worldly wisdom and God's wisdom to prevent contamination, providing context for Origen's later appropriation

label: Crouzel: Origen ranks philosophical schools from worst to best: Epicureans (voluptuous an

metadata.topic: Hierarchy of philosophical schools
metadata.stance: Origen ranks philosophical schools from worst to best: Epicureans (voluptuous and atheistic, at bottom), Peripatetics (deny Providence), Stoics (materialist god, but virtuous), Pythagoreans (metempsychosis), and Platonists (closest to truth, especially regarding knowledge of God)

metadata.topic: Status of Peri Archon

metadata.topic: Origen's priority in the free will-foreknowledge problem
metadata.stance: Origen was almost certainly the second philosopher (after Alexander of Aphrodisias) and the first Christian to discuss the tension between divine foreknowledge and human freedom as a technical philosophical question

metadata.stance: Unlike Alexander of Aphrodisias, Origen maintained that divine foreknowledge was possible and could be communicated through prophetic intermediaries, without compromising human ability to choose otherwise and bear moral responsibility

metadata.topic: Stoic determinism and prophecy

metadata.stance: Origen's discussion of God hardening Pharaoh's heart operates within a Stoic-influenced framework: God's action reveals Pharaoh's pre-existing moral character rather than overriding his choice, with the same divine action having different effects on different dispositions

metadata.topic: Origen against Valentinian determinism
metadata.stance: Origen mocked the Valentinian notion of goodness or badness as essential rather than learned properties, arguing that God hardening Pharaoh's heart indicates 'it was possible for him to obey,' thereby defending the contingency of moral choice against essentialist determinism

engages_with_scholars.note: on proof from prophecy tradition

label: Ramelli: Both Alexander and Origen refuted Stoic determinism using very similar arguments

metadata.topic: Anti-determinism and free will
metadata.stance: Both Alexander and Origen refuted Stoic determinism using very similar arguments, particularly emphasizing praise/blame and the efficacy of petitionary prayer; Alexander deemed Stoic compatibilism between Fate and free will untenable and dangerous for moral life because it excluded responsibility and ruled out to eph' hemin

label: Ramelli: Origen distinguished his Christian doctrine of apokatastasis from Stoic determin

metadata.topic: Origen's distinction between Christian and Stoic apokatastasis
metadata.stance: Origen distinguished his Christian doctrine of apokatastasis from Stoic deterministic apokatastasis in two key ways: (a) the Stoics posited infinite aeons while Origen postulated an end to all aeons; (b) the Stoics held identical repetition while Origen held that each aeon differs due to rational creatures' free choices

engages_with_scholars.note: 2002, on Stoic apokatastasis

supporting_evidence: Stoic doctrine of ekpyrosis and palingenesia

label: Ramelli: Origen refuted Valentinian Gnostic determinism involving predestination of three

metadata.stance: Origen refuted Valentinian Gnostic determinism involving predestination of three classes of humans 'by nature,' which destroyed free will and moral responsibility; this criticism paralleled Alexander's criticism of Stoic determinism

engages_with_scholars.note: 2006, on Gnostic determinism

supporting_evidence: Valentinian Gnostic doctrine of three natures (hylic, psychic, pneumatic)

label: Telfer: The term αὐτεξούσιος evolved from pre-Christian use describing independence (goo

metadata.topic: development of autexousia concept
metadata.stance: The term αὐτεξούσιος evolved from pre-Christian use describing independence (good, neutral, or disparaging tones) to a technical term for moral self-determination; the abstract noun τὸ αὐτεξούσιον emerged only in the second Christian century; by the fourth century, attention shifted from autexousia itself to τρεπτότης (moral precariousness) and the process of moral consolidation toward ἀτρεψία

label: Pouderon: The Greek Apologists (Justin, Tatian, Theophilus, Athenagoras) affirm that God c

metadata.topic: free will (libre arbitre) in Greek Apologists
metadata.stance: The Greek Apologists (Justin, Tatian, Theophilus, Athenagoras) affirm that God created humans and angels with free will (to autexousion), not full freedom like God's, but a free choice enabling them to turn toward either good or evil. This libertarian capacity is central to their theodicy: evil exists as a consequence of God's goodness in granting free choice.
supporting_evidence: Tatian, Oratio ad Graecos (crh'si" pro;" to; kakopoiei'n)
Justin Martyr, various works (series of texts n°9, n°11)

label: Pouderon: God did not create humans naturally or entirely good. The original human was nei

metadata.topic: original human nature as morally neutral
metadata.stance: God did not create humans naturally or entirely good. The original human was neither good nor bad by nature, but capable of receiving either good or evil. This neutral constitution was necessary for the exercise of free will. Tatian pushes this to an extreme, viewing the soul as merely a receptacle of darkness (encratite position).

label: Pouderon: Unlike the Stoics who, according to their adversaries, make God immanent in chan

metadata.topic: Stoic determinism and divine immanence contrasted with Christian free will
metadata.stance: Unlike the Stoics who, according to their adversaries, make God immanent in changeable, passible matter and thus implicate God in evil, the Christian Apologists insist God is not the author of evil. There is no being alongside God who could impose evil as God imposes good.

label: Pouderon: The world is governed by universal law of reason applying to cosmos and individu

metadata.topic: universal law of reason and natural law as oriented toward good
metadata.stance: The world is governed by universal law of reason applying to cosmos and individuals. Humans possess an innate propensity to good through kinship with God (image/resemblance) and individual reason reflecting universal reason. Natural law and right reason turn humans toward good. Justin condemns moral relativism (e.g., sophists) as refusal to admit natural laws and innate sense of good and evil.

label: Pouderon: Creation is governed by Providence—general at the cosmic level, particular at th

metadata.topic: Providence and angelic mediation
metadata.stance: Creation is governed by Providence—general at the cosmic level, particular at the individual level. Particular Providence is delegated to angels, who are passible beings capable of disobedience and sin. This delegation means that the exercise of Providence over humans, entrusted to angels, turned against humanity when angels fell, delivering humans to demonic power and evil domination.

label: Pouderon: Matter is not evil in itself, since a good God created or organized it, and it p

metadata.topic: matter not inherently evil
metadata.stance: Matter is not evil in itself, since a good God created or organized it, and it proceeds from him. Even though partly governed by angels who succumbed to sin, matter's origin in good creation preserves it from inherent evil.

label: Pouderon: Creation contains germs or starting points (sperma, mikra; aphorme) of evil even

metadata.topic: germ/seeds of evil prior to Adam's sin
metadata.stance: Creation contains germs or starting points (sperma, mikra; aphorme) of evil even before Adam's fault—necessary to explain how humans could sin at the instigation of an already fallen being, the serpent. This concept of universal evil in potentiality appears especially in Tatian.
supporting_evidence: Tatian, Oratio ad Graecos (series of texts n°7)

label: Pouderon: God's granting humans the power to freely choose good and evil, which might seem

metadata.topic: pedagogical justification for free will and evil's possibility
metadata.stance: God's granting humans the power to freely choose good and evil, which might seem cruel, is theologically justified as just exercise of Providence. God, with pedagogical intent, wanted to give humans opportunity to improve, amend themselves, and thus merit the gift of life. This is the 'principle of progress' or 'occasion of progressing' (hJ ajformh; prokoph'") emphasized by Theophilus.
supporting_evidence: Theophilus, Ad Autolycum (series of texts n°11)

label: Pouderon: In early Christianity, still heavily imbued with Jewish apocalyptic (Enochic tra

metadata.topic: triple original sin and transmission of evil
metadata.stance: In early Christianity, still heavily imbued with Jewish apocalyptic (Enochic tradition), original sin is triple: (1) corruption of angels who become evil spirits/demons and teach humans sinful practices; (2) disobedience of Adam and Eve, tasting the fruit of knowledge of good and evil, moving from childhood innocence to adult responsibility and guilt; (3) Cain's fratricide introducing murder against humans. This etiological narrative appears in Justin and Athenagoras but not other Apologists.

label: Pouderon: Most Apologists make Adam's sin essentially a sin of disobedience—violation of a

metadata.topic: Adam's sin as disobedience, not concupiscence or pride
metadata.stance: Most Apologists make Adam's sin essentially a sin of disobedience—violation of a benevolent Creator's prohibition. It is not associated with sexual concupiscence, pretension to become gods (which they already are in some sense), or unhealthy curiosity/desire to know as much as God (periergia).

label: Pouderon: One weakened sense of 'original sin' is the prototype or first sin destined to e

metadata.topic: communication of sin through example and imitation
metadata.stance: One weakened sense of 'original sin' is the prototype or first sin destined to entail others. The most banal principle of communication is example (arche) and imitation (mimesis): humans sin following Satan and demons' example; commit murder following Cain's example. Arche here means not merely temporal priority but a principle, starting point necessarily calling for continuation—the path is open, traced, calling errant travelers.

label: Pouderon: Justin insists on the 'bath' of sin into which humans are plunged from birth, wh

metadata.topic: bath of sin and baptismal cleansing
metadata.stance: Justin insists on the 'bath' of sin into which humans are plunged from birth, which can only be erased through baptismal bath. It remains unclear whether this refers to the child's moral environment marked by concupiscence presiding over generation, imprinted with surrounding vices and society's vices, or to inheritance of Adam's sin.

label: Pouderon: Adam and Eve's fault profoundly transformed human nature. The main consequence i

metadata.topic: transformation of human nature through punishment
metadata.stance: Adam and Eve's fault profoundly transformed human nature. The main consequence is intrusion of biological necessities: suffering, illness, bodily desires and needs, and death. These biological necessities, fruits of initial fault, affect human essence itself.

metadata.stance: Philo's position resembles Plato's Timaeus in structure (universal soul governing world, rational/irrational souls in conflict in man), but differs crucially: in Plato, victory of reason or passions depends entirely on relative strength/weakness, making outcomes seem determined by these factors plus external causes. The text breaks off before Wolfson fully develops the contrast with Philo's position, but implies Philo allows more genuine contingency or moral freedom

engages_with_scholars.note: Wolfson argues Philo is essentially based on Plato but with significant differences on whether rational/irrational victory is determined by relative strength

label: Vibe: Philo's notion of human freedom must be elucidated through his concept of necess

metadata.topic: Philo's concept of human freedom
metadata.stance: Philo's notion of human freedom must be elucidated through his concept of necessity, and derives from the Platonic tradition rather than the Stoic tradition. Human freedom manifests as self-determination (αὐτοκελεύστου γνώμης) opposed to other-determination, specifically freedom from necessity (ἀνάγκη) that prevents self-determination.

engages_with_scholars.note: Wolfson argued Philo means absolutely undetermined freedom like God's, with power to upset laws of causality; Vibe argues this must be modified by Platonic rather than Stoic framework

Winston argued Philo adapts Stoic notion of relative free will; Vibe agrees relative freedom is correct but argues the source is Platonic not Stoic, and that Winston's 'evidently deterministic' reading needs modification because Philo describes limited human ἑκούσιον as capacity to rule over necessity

Radice argued Philo stresses human freedom in matters of morality and accepts communion/cosmic sympathy while confuting Chaldean pantheism; Vibe finds this needs further elaboration on Philo's reservations about Stoic cosmic sympathy
Frick noted Philo rules out necessity in matters of morality but also has deterministic train of thought; cited via Radice
Niehoff pointed out Philo's notion of divine bonds holding cosmos together echoes Plato's Timaeus; Vibe uses this to argue Philo opposes Stoic cosmology and insists on God's transcendence
Sellars on Stoic cosmic sympathy as product of pneuma permeating cosmos, arranged into necessary series of causes admitting no exceptions
mentioned as recent book at end of excerpt

supporting_evidence: Philo, Deus Imm. 47-49: God gave birth to the mind and judged it worthy of freedom (αὐτὴν [διάνοια] ὁ γεννήσας πατὴρ ἐλευθερίας ἠξίωσε); human beings received spontaneous and self-determining mind (ἐθελουργοῦ καὶ αὐτοκελεύστου γνώμης λαχών); God created each human as free and unfettered (ἄφετον καὶ ἐλεύθερον) who uses powers of action by voluntary and deliberate choices (ἑκουσίοις καὶ πραιρετικαῖς)
Philo, Somn. 2.253: ὁ μὲν θεὸς ἑκούσιον, ἀνάγκη δὲ ἡ οὐσία — God is free will, the created is necessity

Philo, Rer. Div. Her. 301: Moses understood causes have sequence, connection and interplay (ἀκολουθίαν μὲν καὶ εἱρμὸν καὶ ἐπιπλοκὰς αἰτιῶν) but did not refer to these as causes of events; the true cause is someone older and antecedent (πρεσβύτερον ἄλλο ἐποχούμενον τοῖς ὅλοις), compared to charioteer or captain
Philo, Migr. Abr. 181: powers that hold universe together
Plato, Timaeus: demiurge keeps cosmos bound together and protects from destruction

label: Vibe: Philo's necessity (ἀνάγκη) derives from Platonic tradition, not Stoic fate (εἰμα

metadata.topic: Philo's concept of necessity
metadata.stance: Philo's necessity (ἀνάγκη) derives from Platonic tradition, not Stoic fate (εἰμαρμένη). It represents that which prevents human beings from living as self-determining creatures. Freedom from necessity may refer to freedom from inherent potential for destruction that characterizes created reality (where creation implies destruction), not exemption from Stoic causal laws. God is exempt from laws of nature, not laws of Stoic fate.

engages_with_scholars.note: Winston described Philo's ethical thought as 'evidently deterministic' and saw Stoic influence; Vibe argues Philo's description of transcendent God as exempt from laws of nature (creation implies destruction) means he is not describing exemption from Stoic fate laws
Niehoff's observation that Philo's divine bonds echo Plato's Timaeus supports Vibe's argument that Philo opposes Stoic cosmology

supporting_evidence: Philo, Deus Imm. 47-48: necessity prevents self-determination

Philo, Somn. 2.129-130: individual from ruling class in Alexandria claimed power of constraining necessity (εἰμαρμένης ἀνάγκης δύναμις); Philo criticizes this as blasphemous divine pretension but does not presume such constraining necessity exists
Philo, Quaest. in Gen. 1.21: Adam naming animals typifies 'all that is voluntary in us, thus confounding those who say that all things exist by...'
Philo, Rer. Div. Her. 300: denies fate and necessity are αἰτίας γινομένων ἁπάντων (causes of everything that happens)
Plato, Timaeus: demiurge binds cosmos together, protecting from destruction

label: Maston: Argues that the Hodayot present a radically different model where human creature

metadata.topic: predestination and human incapacity in the Hodayot
metadata.stance: Argues that the Hodayot present a radically different model where human creaturely existence entails fundamental weakness—both material and moral. metadata.stance: Contends that Romans 7:7-25 critiques the 'two-ways theology' exemplified by Sirach—specifically the confidence that humans can obey Torah and thereby attain life. label: Maston: Acknowledges that even in more deterministic texts like the Hodayot, some form o

metadata.stance: Acknowledges that even in more deterministic texts like the Hodayot, some form of human response remains meaningful within the predetermined structure. Paul's discourse about the Spirit and human agency operates without any libertarian free will vocabulary.

label: Helm: Defends 'theistic compatibilism' or 'Creatorly compatibilism' as distinct from p

metadata.topic: theological compatibilism
metadata.stance: Defends 'theistic compatibilism' or 'Creatorly compatibilism' as distinct from philosophical determinism. God's ordination and sustaining of all things is not identical to creaturely determinism but is consistent with human moral responsibility. The divine causation operates through transcendent rather than immanent causal relations.

label: Jewett: The 'I' in Romans 7:13-25 is a speech-in-character (προσωποποιία) depicting Paul

metadata.topic: free will and moral agency in Romans 7
metadata.stance: The 'I' in Romans 7:13-25 is a speech-in-character (προσωποποιία) depicting Paul's preconversion zealotism, not a description of the normal Christian life or universal human moral psychology. The passage portrays a divided self where sin, not the person, is the active agent responsible for evil actions (vv. 17, 20), while the 'I' retains moral identification with the good through the mind's delight in God's law (v. 22). The person 'left to himself' (v. 25b-c) remains enslaved to sin's law in the flesh despite willing the good, indicating that without divine intervention through Christ, moral achievement of the good is impossible.

engages_with_scholars.note: Rejects Bultmann's claim that v. 25b-c contradicts earlier argument by replacing agreement with law with 'serving the law'
Disagrees with Lichtenberger's view that v. 25b-c reflects continued presence of sin in believers (simul iustus et peccator) and that it constitutes an interpolation altering Paul's argument
Rejects Käsemann's claim that v. 25b-c implies non-Pauline anthropological dualism between mind and flesh

label: Jewett: Paul's use of the subjunctive 'let us have peace' (εἰρήνην ἔχωμεν) constitutes a

metadata.topic: free will and human response to divine grace
metadata.stance: Paul's use of the subjunctive 'let us have peace' (εἰρήνην ἔχωμεν) constitutes an admonition requiring active human response to God's offer of righteousness, rather than a triumphalist indicative assertion that believers already possess peace. The formulation implies that having been justified by faith, believers must still make the necessary response to embody this peace concretely in congregational life.

engages_with_scholars.note: Jewett rejects the theological argument that peace is a gift that cannot be merited, which has led most commentaries to reject the subjunctive reading
cited for chiastic pattern analysis in vv. 6-8

label: Jewett: The peace Paul enjoins has significant social implications; the house and teneme

metadata.topic: moral responsibility and congregational behavior
metadata.stance: The peace Paul enjoins has significant social implications; the house and tenement churches in Rome are acting in combative manners against one another, showing they have not yet embodied the peace Paul has in mind. The first person plural formulation includes all members of Paul's audience as responsible agents who must actively respond to God's initiative.

label: Jewett: The passive voice of δικαιωθέντες ('having been set right') indicates righteousn

metadata.topic: determinism vs. human agency in salvation
metadata.stance: The passive voice of δικαιωθέντες ('having been set right') indicates righteousness as divine gift, yet this does not eliminate human agency. The aorist passive participle refers to a past event (baptism or conversion) that extended righteousness to all believers, but the subsequent subjunctive exhortations ('let us have peace,' 'let us boast') require ongoing active response. No person or group can stand before God on achievements or prior status, but only on the basis of grace—yet this grace demands concrete embodiment in life.

metadata.topic: the role of the law in stimulating sin
metadata.stance: The law, when misunderstood as a means of earning salvation, becomes an unbearable yoke that actually stimulates sinful passions; true freedom comes through death to the law in Christ's body, enabling service in newness of the Spirit.

label: Hendriksen: The passage reflects Paul's own experience and that of others like him—the strug

metadata.topic: Paul's autobiographical interpretation of Romans 7:7-25
metadata.stance: The passage reflects Paul's own experience and that of others like him—the struggle of the 'wretched man' who is ultimately rescued through Jesus Christ, indicating a progression from bondage under law to victory in Christ.

label: Hendriksen: Affirms that divine predestination is a central doctrine in Romans 9–11, foresha

metadata.topic: divine predestination and election
metadata.stance: Affirms that divine predestination is a central doctrine in Romans 9–11, foreshadowed in 8:29–30 and developed in 9:10–24 and 11:5–8, 29. God's election operates on the basis of sovereign grace rather than human merit, as illustrated by the cases of Jacob and Esau (9:6–18).

engages_with_scholars.note: Acknowledges that many able scholars, both past and present, interpret Rom. 9–11 as referring to a future comprehensive eschatological salvation of the nation Israel as a whole, but Hendriksen indicates this will be discussed and appears skeptical of this reading

label: Hendriksen: Emphasizes that salvation is entirely by faith apart from works of the law, with

metadata.topic: justification by faith vs. works/merit
metadata.stance: Emphasizes that salvation is entirely by faith apart from works of the law, with no room for human boasting. The Jews misunderstood God's promises as conditioned on human merit and natural descent from Abraham, rather than on divine grace alone.

label: Hendriksen: While affirming divine sovereign grace as the source of salvation, Hendriksen no

metadata.topic: free will and human responsibility in salvation
metadata.stance: While affirming divine sovereign grace as the source of salvation, Hendriksen notes that Israel's rejection was 'because of its unbelief' (9:27, 31, 32; 10:21), suggesting human unbelief as the cause of rejection. However, he also emphasizes that salvation is 'the product not of human works or merit but of divine sovereign grace.' The tension between divine sovereignty and human unbelief is acknowledged but not systematically resolved.

label: Hendriksen: Presents the potter-clay imagery as illustrating God's sovereign right to make '

metadata.topic: potter and clay metaphor (Rom. 9:19–24)
metadata.stance: Presents the potter-clay imagery as illustrating God's sovereign right to make 'one vessel for honor and another for dishonor' out of the same lump, emphasizing divine prerogative in election and rejection. This is framed under the section 'God's Wrath and Mercy.'

label: Hendriksen: Maintains that salvation is available to all without ethnic distinction, through

metadata.topic: scope of salvation: Jew and Gentile
metadata.stance: Maintains that salvation is available to all without ethnic distinction, through faith alone. The Gentiles are saved in the same way as Jews, and the disobedience of the Jews opens salvation to Gentiles, while Gentile salvation provokes Jewish jealousy that leads to salvation—for the elect remnant in both cases.

metadata.topic: human agency and divine action in justification
metadata.stance: Paul's 'rectification by faith' (ek pisteōs) refers primarily to God's faithful action that generates human trust, not to an individual virtue or intellectual conviction; faith is 'strengthened by God' and evidenced in Abraham's confidence in God's promise

metadata.topic: cosmic scope of salvation and human enslavement to powers
metadata.stance: The human situation involves enslavement to cosmic powers of Sin and Death that have invaded the entire human cosmos; peace with God results not simply from reconciliation between God and humans but from the defeat of these powers through Christ's death and resurrection

label: Gaventa: The repeated use of 'all' in 5:12-21 warns against limiting God's actions to tho

metadata.topic: universal scope of God's action and warning against presumption
metadata.stance: The repeated use of 'all' in 5:12-21 warns against limiting God's actions to those who presently constitute the 'we'; God's actions are not confined to those who presently believe, anticipating the discussion of God's dealings with offspring in chapters 9-11
supporting_evidence: Romans 11:17-24 (engrafting of gentiles, not replacement of Israel)

label: Gaventa: The Spirit's work transforms 'slaves of righteousness' into siblings of Jesus Ch

metadata.topic: Spirit's liberating work and transformation of human status
metadata.stance: The Spirit's work transforms 'slaves of righteousness' into siblings of Jesus Christ, with creation anticipating God's final triumph; this liberation is not merely individual moral improvement but cosmic redemption
supporting_evidence: Romans 8:21 (hope for glory of God's children)

label: Hendriksen: Paul teaches a sequential divine decree: foreknowledge leads to foreordination,

metadata.topic: divine foreordination and human calling
metadata.stance: Paul teaches a sequential divine decree: foreknowledge leads to foreordination, which leads to calling, justification, and glorification; this golden chain (Rom 8:29-30) demonstrates God's sovereign purpose in salvation, with believers being 'called according to his purpose' (8:28)

engages_with_scholars.note: Cites Calvin's Institutes III.xi.6 on the inseparability of justification and sanctification

label: Hendriksen: The 'mind of the flesh' is hostile to God and 'cannot' submit to God's law (7:7)

metadata.topic: human moral inability and the Spirit's enabling
metadata.stance: The 'mind of the flesh' is hostile to God and 'cannot' submit to God's law (7:7); those 'in the flesh' 'cannot please God' (8:8). This indicates a genuine moral inability that requires the Spirit's regenerating work for freedom. The believer experiences simultaneous bondage to sin's presence and freedom through the Spirit's power.

label: Hendriksen: Creation was subjected to futility 'not by its own choice' (8:20), indicating th

metadata.topic: creation's subjection to futility and hope
metadata.stance: Creation was subjected to futility 'not by its own choice' (8:20), indicating that non-rational creation experiences a bondage to decay imposed by God's design, yet with hope of future liberation. This parallels the believer's present groaning and future redemption.
supporting_evidence: Romans 8:20 'it was not by its own choice that the creation was subjected to futility, but because of him who subjected it, in hope'

label: Hendriksen: The Christian life involves 'three groanings'—creation, believers themselves, an

metadata.topic: believer's present struggle and future victory
metadata.stance: The Christian life involves 'three groanings'—creation, believers themselves, and the Spirit—all pointing to eager expectation of future glory. Despite present suffering and weakness, believers are 'more than conquerors' (8:37) through Christ's love, with all things working together for good for those who love God and are called according to his purpose.

metadata.stance: The idiosyncratic history of Israel's creation in Romans 9:6-13 insists on God's creation 'without reference to Israel's goodness, faith, obedience, or even potential,' setting a tone of divine initiative that runs through the argument; yet this does not negate human responsibility as the argument develops toward warnings against gentile arrogance and the final doxology

metadata.topic: fate and eschatological promise
metadata.stance: The overarching question of Romans 9-11 is 'where Israel belongs in God's eschatological victory,' with the conclusion insisting on God's provision for 'all Israel' (11:26) and warning against false claims to understand God's mind; the 'impossible' character of God's mercy ultimately prevails over apparent rejection

metadata.stance: Paul presents the Mosaic law as a dominating, lord-like power (kyrieuein) that holds people in bondage, analogous to Sin and Death; believers are 'released from the law' through death with Christ to serve 'in the newness of the spirit' rather than 'the oldness of the letter'

metadata.stance: Paul's argument presupposes that moral agents cannot live under two competing regimes simultaneously; the believer's transfer from 'under law' to 'under grace' involves a fundamental change of lordship that affects moral possibility—freedom from the law's dominion enables new moral fruit-bearing for God

metadata.stance: Paul presents a paradoxical dynamic where the law itself arouses sinful passions (7:5), yet the law is not simply identified with Sin; this creates tension in Paul's account of moral agency—the law is not Sin, but it functions within a deterministic-like economy where 'while we were in the flesh, the sinful passions aroused by the law were at work in our limbs, bearing fruit for Death'

metadata.stance: Paul depicts humanity as under the powerful grip of Sin and Death, with Sin able to make use of God's holy law, inhabit the human body, and create a fissure in the law itself (Romans 7:7-25); this enslavement is not merely abstract but involves real power dynamics

label: Gaventa: God's action in Christ Jesus liberates humanity from enslavement to Sin and Deat

metadata.topic: divine liberation and human agency
metadata.stance: God's action in Christ Jesus liberates humanity from enslavement to Sin and Death through the Spirit; this liberation is an event initiated by God's power, not human action. The Spirit actively intercedes for humans and produces life, peace, and adoption. Human participation is secondary and responsive: believers 'put to death the actions of the body by the Spirit' (8:13), but the primary agency is God's

label: Gaventa: Gaventa notes that in Romans 8:1, 'nothing is said here about faith as a qualify

metadata.topic: faith as condition for liberation
metadata.stance: Gaventa notes that in Romans 8:1, 'nothing is said here about faith as a qualifying factor' and 'the language of faith has slipped off the screen.' However, she qualifies that pistis as trust in God's action is 'at the heart of what it means to be "in Christ"' based on earlier references (1:16; 3:22; 5:1). The phrase 'in Christ Jesus' signals a locative transfer from one realm to another rather than a human achievement

label: Gaventa: The law is rendered powerless (adynaton) by the flesh/Sin's power, but God acts

metadata.topic: the law's powerlessness and God's power
metadata.stance: The law is rendered powerless (adynaton) by the flesh/Sin's power, but God acts through the Spirit that yields life in Christ Jesus. God's power (dynamis) is the central theme of Romans, from Christ's resurrection (1:4) through the gospel (1:16) to Abraham's confidence (4:21) and the culminating assurance of 8:38-39. The law's right demand is fulfilled not by the law itself or by human effort, but by those who live 'conformed to the Spirit'

label: Gaventa: The singular 'you' in 8:2 is surprising and deliberately addresses the 'I' of 7:

metadata.topic: the 'I' of Romans 7 and the address to 'you'
metadata.stance: The singular 'you' in 8:2 is surprising and deliberately addresses the 'I' of 7:7-25; Paul turns to address the enslaved 'I' with a word of liberation. This suggests the 'I' represents a real voice of enslaved humanity rather than merely a rhetorical device, and God's liberation is directed personally to the one caught in this bondage

label: Barclay: Mirror-reading is essential but extremely problematic; scholars must account for

metadata.topic: methodology of mirror-reading polemical texts
metadata.stance: Mirror-reading is essential but extremely problematic; scholars must account for Paul's indirect address to opponents through the Galatians, the distorting effects of polemic, and the hermeneutical circularity of interpreting statements without knowing the opponents' linguistic context.
